word_order: SOV — verbs and predicates consistently appear at clause end (e.g. '휴학 생각하고 있거든', '친구들이랑 고기를 먹고 헤어졌는데'), with objects/complements preceding the verb.
punctuation_present: sometimes — some sentences end with '.', '?' (e.g. 2, 5, 9, 10, 14, 16, 17, 18) but many transcribed utterances have no terminal punctuation at all (e.g. 1, 3, 4, 8, 11, 15).
register: spontaneous conversational speech (casual dialogue/interview transcript, disfluent, with repetitions and self-corrections)
non_boundary_traps: 이제 (frequently a filler, not a true temporal clause marker)
그 그 / 두 두 / 딴 딴 (stutter-repetitions, not separate clauses)
그거 (vague filler pronoun, not a referential boundary)
target_language_risks: Pro-drop: subjects/objects are frequently omitted and must be inferred from prior context, risking incomplete English sentences if segmented too early
Sentence-final particles (-거든, -잖아, -지) encode speaker attitude/certainty that has no direct English equivalent and can be lost if segment is cut mid-clause
SOV order means the verb (often the key meaning-bearing element) appears late; early segmentation before the verb can produce mistranslated or verb-less English fragments
Honorific/politeness level differences are not recoverable once segmented, risking flattened register in English
Self-repairs and false starts (repeated words, trailing off clauses) can be mistaken for real clause boundaries, causing fragmented or nonsensical English output
notes_for_prompt_writer: Treat this as disfluent spoken Korean: rely on connective endings (-는데, -고, -니까, -거든, -잖아) and sentence-final particles/punctuation as the primary segmentation cues, not on spacing or fillers. Do not split at 이제, 막, 그, or stutter-repeats, as these are discourse fillers, not clause boundaries. Because Korean is strongly head-final (verb-final), delay segmentation until after the verb/predicate is reached to preserve meaning for English SVO reconstruction.
